abstract: Extracellular vesicle (EV) heterogeneity is well established, but how distinct EV populations emerge from the same donor cell remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated plasma membrane organization as a potential contributor to EV molecular heterogeneity in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). CD133/PROM1 expression was associated with plasma membrane remodeling, including prominent protrusion formation, and with the redistribution of the EV-associated tetraspanin CD63 toward these domains. Quantitative immunogold electron microscopy revealed a disproportionate enrichment of CD63 labeling within protrusions following CD133 expression. This remodeling was accompanied by increased EV particle output and altered EV-associated marker signals. Single-particle analysis identified distinct CD133/CD63, CD133/CD63-, and CD133-/CD63 EV populations, demonstrating that CD133 and CD63 were not uniformly distributed across detected EVs. CD63 was detected more frequently in the CD133 than in the CD133- EV fraction, supporting an association between CD133 expression and EV marker heterogeneity. CD133 expression was also associated with changes in intracellular multivesicular body (MVB) density and size distribution, with different responses across the two TNBC cell models examined. Together, these findings suggest that plasma membrane organization may contribute to EV heterogeneity alongside context-dependent remodeling of intracellular MVB compartments. Rather than implicating CD133 in a single EV biogenesis pathway, our data highlight spatial membrane organization as a potential determinant of EV molecular diversity.
